Getty Images By Caitlin KennySpecial to the Star Side part! No, centre part. Wait … back to side part.For all the group-chat discourse, TikTok hot takes and millennial existential crises that the hair-parting pendulum spurred, it overlooked a major truth: that wearing your hair down doesn’t need to be such a dichotomy. A lot of us stick to our go-to look day after day — so much so that the suggestion to shift our part by a couple inches feels radical. But what if this spring, instead of debating which part is back “in,” we just … switched up our hair style regularly?To be fair, there’s a reason we find ourselves locked in on a signature look: “If you’ve got a set schedule and you know you can do the same old, same old in 25 minutes and it will look the way you expect it to, there isn’t great motivation to try something new,” says Toronto-based hairstylist Ashley Readings.Aside from the good ol’ fun of experimenting with hairstyles (like the joy of wearing a new outfit, but without the hit to your credit card bill), there’s a protective factor too. “A lot of the damage our hair suffers is from repetition,” says Readings. “Many people struggle to see hair growth around their face-framing layers because they focus their hot tools on those pieces and if they don’t change their part or style, they get damaged more than the rest.” ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW To get you started, we put together a week’s worth of different ways to wear your hair down, with tips from Readings to get it done easily and quickly. Bella Hadid, Gillian Anderson. Getty Images A Throwback HeadbandThe look: With “Love Story” spurring a Carolyn Bessette Kennedy style revival, we’re clamouring for tortoiseshell headbands again. Miu Miu’s fall 2026 runway also made a strong case for the stretchy comb ones from our grade-school days (a look so good Gillian Anderson wore it down the catwalk then kept it on even after the show). “Headbands are a saviour when you want to extend a blow dry, suffer from greasy roots or are leaving a workout class,” says Readings. “You can push it back out of your face and still benefit from the style in the lengths of your hair, whether that means heat-styled strands or natural texture.”The effort level: Zero.The styling tip: If you have short hair and a headband that goes all the way around, it might cause the strands at the nape of your neck to stick up awkwardly. Readings recommends pushing it away from your neck, and then using a tail comb to pull out those pieces so they sit under the band instead. “The classic headband that only sits on the top of the head requires no tips — they are that easy.”The tools: Kitsch Tort Wide Headband, $20, mykitsch.ca. Photo: KitschShop Here Quo Beauty Stretch Comb Headbands, $7 for three, shoppersdrugmart.ca. Photo: Quo BeautyShop Here Margot Robbie, Zendaya. Getty Images The Tight Ear-TuckThe look: This ultra-flattering look (hello, cheekbones) is basically just hair worn down and side-parted, but with extra asymmetry thanks to the sleekness on one side. Even better: it works with any length and style — blown out, waved, curled or air-dried.The effort level: Got an extra five minutes?The styling tip: You want this to look a little sharper than simply tucking one side behind your ear. Readings recommends using gel and an edge comb to smooth hair down, and using a tiny elastic to tie the “tucked” section to hair back near the nape of your neck. It will be hidden by the rest of your hair that falls overtop. Want even easier? “Break out the French combs that hairstylist Guido Palau used for The Row’s spring show,” suggests Readings.The tools: Fenty Beauty The Gelly Type Strong Hold Gel, $39, sephora.com. Photo: Fenty BeautyShop Here Quo Beauty Hair Combs, $8 for eight, shoppersdrugmart.ca Photo: Quo BeautyShop Here Sarah Pidgeon, Lisa. Getty Images Romantic Half-Up WavesThe look: Consider this another mega-easy style that works on any texture of hair — and with any accessory you have lying around. “This look was made for all those expensive claw clips and scrunchies we bought during the pandemic,” says Readings. If you just have a plain old elastic, she recommends pulling hair only halfway through on the last loop to keep the vibe casual. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW The effort level: Taking candy from a baby.The styling tip: Let any shorter layers fall forward, and leave the hair around your ears loose. “Don’t get too precious about it,” says Readings. “Try doing this without looking in the mirror because I bet it will come out better than having too many expectations.”The tools: Simons Large Monarch Clip, $15, simons.ca. Photo: SimonsShop Here Cake Beauty The Big Wig Dry Texturizing Spray, $13, shoppersdrugmart.ca. Photo: Cake BeautyShop Here Olivia Dean, Elle Fanning. Getty Images Brushed-Out WavesThe look: For this hairstyle tiny action equals big impact: “Brushing out waves completely changes the look,” says Readings. She loves first curling hair away from the face with a small-barrelled curing iron, then taking a brush to it. “The shape becomes something almost triangular and there is a nod to vintage styling that doesn’t feel like a costume.”The effort level: Just a hint for the curling-iron action (or you can brush out natural curls and get a different style but the same great volume).The styling tip: “For someone with slicker, straighter hair, indulge the shape with a volumizing hairspray,” says Readings. “If you have naturally curly hair, frizz can take over a brush-out, so focus on a spray wax and shine oil to give it a bit of weight.” And if your ends are needing some TLC, skip this style till you’ve had a fresh trim.The tools: Amika Rising Star Hair Volumizing Finishing Spray, $44, sephora.com. Photo: AmikaShop Here JVN Complete Nourishing Hair Oil Shine Drops, $35.50, sephora.com. Photo: JVNShop Here Kerry Washington, Jessica Williams. Getty Images Retro VolumeThe look: Play with contrast by building major volume at the crown and pulling everything ultra tight up in front. Take a page from Shrinking’s Jessica Williams with a half-up style (bonus points for the bow), or conceal the pulled-back parts à la Kerry Washington. “Kerry’s hair is most likely pulled into a bun towards the top of her hair, then with a full or half wig pinned into it,” says Readings.The effort level: Medium — go for this one when you’ve got a little extra time. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW The styling tip: Get that major root boost with volumizing powder and gentle backcombing, then smooth out the front. “Whether you want a part in the hair or to have it all pulled back, it’s about breaking out a strong hold gel and an edge comb,” says Readings. Her go-to tool? “The Pattern edge comb should be in every single person’s bathroom — I have about six of them because they are so good.”The tools: DesignMe Puff.Me Volumizing Powder, $31, amazon.ca. Photo: DesignMeShop Here Pattern Edge Tool, $17.50, sephora.com. Photo: PatternShop Here Sabrina Carpenter, Kate Hudson. Getty Images One Little PinThe look: Next time you want to flip your part way over, add a pin — both pretty and practical. “I love this because changing your part can be a struggle,” says Readings. “The pin allows you to move your hair to a different side and have it swoop low across your face rather than up and over.”The effort level: Negative one.The styling tip: “Keep the pin around your eyebrow height and angle it upwards,” says Readings. To help it stay in place, she recommends giving the clip a spritz of hairspray for extra grip.The tools: Ardene 4-Pack Pearl & Rhinestone Hair Pins, $4.90, ardene.com. Photo: ArdeneShop Here Tresemmé A-list Workable Hairspray, $13.50, amazon.ca. Photo: TresemméShop Here Amanda Seyfried, Gwyneth Paltrow. Getty Images A Perfectly Placed BendThe look: “This style mimics the way the hair is tucked behind the ear with a centre part and can also give the illusion of layers,” says Readings. “The bends open up the hair in the same spots that face-framing layers would sit, at the cheekbones and jawline.”The effort level: Hot tools but make it easy.The styling tip: “You’re just ‘suggesting’ a wave, so keep the heat low and the hot tool moving quickly,” says Readings. You can use a flat iron or curling iron to create bends at the cheekbones and just below the jawline, but don’t clamp down too hard. “Skipping heat on the ends of your hair will make the style much more lived-in,” says Readings. “Or round the ends with a bigger curling iron for something more polished.”The tools: Typebea S1 Ultimate Styling Serum, $37, sephora.com. Photo: TypeabeaShop Here Conair 1” Double Ceramic Flat Iron, $30, amazon.ca. Photo: ConairShop HereWhen you make a purchase through the links in this article, we may earn a small commission.
